home.lead: A VPN the anoni.net community runs for the people around it, so you can get online with confidence where VPNs often fail: at school, in hotels, abroad.

how.title: How it works
how.1.title: Redeem an invite
how.1.body: Enter your invite code and you get a 16-digit account number. You sign in with it from then on.
how.2.title: Add a device
how.2.body: Pick the city of the node, name the device, and choose whether to block malicious sites and ads.

when.title: When it helps
when.1.title: Public Wi-Fi
when.1.body: On Wi-Fi at a café, hotel or school, whoever runs the network cannot see which sites you visit.
when.2.title: Trips abroad
when.2.body: Connections are disguised, so they get through more easily on networks that block VPNs. Before you leave, install the app, create the device and test the connection at home. Some places restrict VPNs, so read the FAQ before you go.
when.3.title: Blocked sites
when.3.body: Sites your network blocks have a better chance of opening through a Vessel node.
when.4.title: Scams and phishing
when.4.body: Choose Block malware when you create a device, and scam, phishing and malware sites on the lists will not open. A site that has just appeared may not be listed yet.
when.5.title: Ads and trackers
when.5.body: Choose Block malware, ads and trackers, and many ads and trackers in apps and web pages will not load.
when.6.title: Home and mobile data
when.6.body: Once you are on Vessel, your mobile carrier or internet provider sees only a connection to Vessel, not which sites you visit.
when.note: Vessel protects the connection between you and Vessel's server. It does not make you anonymous: Vessel's server can see which sites you visit, and the accounts you sign in to still know it is you. When you need anonymity, use Tor Browser.
works.title: How Vessel works
works.lists: Before your device opens a site, it looks up the site's address. For a device with a filter, Vessel checks the address against public lists such as HaGeZi's, one after another; listed sites are blocked, and the rest open as usual.
works.disguise: A plain VPN carries the same header on every connection, so networks that inspect traffic recognise and block it easily. Vessel runs on the open-source AmneziaWG, which handles the disguise and the connection, so its packets have nothing steady to recognise.
works.relay: When connecting straight to a node is unstable, you can pick a relay route: the connection goes to an entry in Taipei first, which forwards it as it is to the node. The entry never opens the tunnel, and the exit is still the node's city.
works.keys: When you add a device, the keys for its connection are made in your browser. The private key exists only in your config file; the portal and the node get only the public key, and the account needs no email.
why.title: Why the community runs it
why.body: People often ask the community which VPN to use. We saw how getting online goes at school, in hotels and abroad, and wanted a service we could recommend to the people around us without hesitation, so we put the community's skills into building Vessel. It costs nothing to use. Partners who support the community fund its development and running costs.
why.reach: Someone reads every piece of feedback, and the state of the service is public on the status page.

faq.title: Frequently asked questions
faq.art.title: What each layer can see
faq.invite.q: How do I get an invite code?
faq.invite.a: For now, codes go out through the anoni.net newsletter, one per subscriber. If you did not get the newsletter, write to whisper@anoni.net, or tell us on the feedback page and leave a way to reach you, saying what you need. Places are limited, and codes go out in rounds depending on how the service is used.
faq.cost.a: No. Vessel is a service the community runs for the people around it, and partners who support the community fund its development and running costs.
faq.lost.q: What if I lose my account number?
faq.lost.a: The service has no email for you and stores only a hash of the number that cannot be reversed, so an old number cannot be recovered. With a passkey, sign in with it and get a new number on the account page. Without one, you need a new invite code. We suggest keeping the number in a password manager.
faq.number.q: The account number is only digits. Is that safe?
faq.number.a: Sixteen digits give ten quadrillion combinations, and sign-in attempts are rate limited, so guessing is not practical. The database stores only a keyed hash of the number, which is hard to reverse even if the database leaks.
faq.passkey.a: A passkey replaces a password. It lives in your password manager or security key, such as iCloud Keychain, Google Password Manager or Bitwarden, and syncs with it, so it stays with you when you change phones. You sign in by unlocking your phone or computer; the service keeps only the public key and never gets your fingerprint or face. Add one on the account page, and use it to get a new account number. Tor Browser cannot use most passkeys yet, so sign in with your account number there.
faq.share.q: Can my family use my account?
faq.share.a: An account holds up to 3 devices sharing 50 GB a month, so family devices are fine. Anyone with the account number can also see and delete your devices, so share it only with people you trust. Accounts and invite codes must not be sold.
faq.protocols.q: How do VPN, WireGuard and AmneziaWG relate?
faq.protocols.a: VPN is the general name for services that send your connection through another server before it goes out. VPNs connect in different ways, called protocols, and WireGuard is one of them: simple, fast and used by many VPN apps. AmneziaWG is an open-source project built from WireGuard that adds a disguise, so connections are harder to recognize as a VPN and get through more easily on networks that block VPNs. Vessel uses AmneziaWG.
faq.maker.a: The Amnezia team, and its code is public on GitHub for anyone to check. Vessel has no direct affiliation with Amnezia. Get the app from its official store page or GitHub; the links in the setup steps all point to official sources.
faq.app.q: Why can't I use the regular WireGuard® app?
faq.app.a: Vessel disguises its connections with AmneziaWG, so its packets look different from regular WireGuard, and the regular app cannot use the config.
faq.disguise.a: In tests with the open-source traffic analyser nDPI, plain WireGuard is classified as a VPN and Vessel as QUIC web traffic. Equipment that matches packet patterns has a hard time recognising Vessel, but equipment that analyses traffic more deeply may still recognise it. The disguise lowers the chance of being blocked; it does not guarantee that every network lets you connect. If a network will not let you connect, tell us on the feedback page, and we will use it to adjust the disguise.
faq.ios.q: AmneziaWG is missing from my App Store
faq.ios.a: It is listed in Taiwan, Hong Kong and Japan. In the few regions where it is missing, you can download it with an Apple ID from another region; iPhones have no other way to install it. On Android you can install the APK instead.
faq.androidVpn.q: Android says the VPN service was not authorized?
faq.androidVpn.a: Android allows one VPN at a time, and the most common cause is another VPN app with Always-on VPN turned on. Go to Settings → Network & internet → VPN, tap the gear next to that app, and turn off Always-on VPN and Block connections without VPN. If you pressed cancel on the confirmation window earlier, open AmneziaWG and tap the switch in the app, and the window appears again.
faq.androidBackground.q: On Android, the VPN stops when I close AmneziaWG?
faq.androidBackground.a: On some Android phones, swiping AmneziaWG away from Recent apps also closes the VPN. Leave the app with the home button instead, and the tunnel stays connected. You can also go to Settings → Network & internet → VPN, tap the gear next to AmneziaWG and turn on Always-on VPN, so the VPN reconnects when the system closes it.
faq.twoDevices.q: Can I use one config on two devices?
faq.twoDevices.a: No. Two devices connected at once keep taking the connection from each other and drop out often. Create a config for each device, up to 3 per account.
faq.newPhone.q: What about a new phone or a reinstall?
faq.newPhone.a: A config is shown only once, when it is created, and the service's servers do not have the private key. Delete the old device from your list and create a new one.
faq.filter.q: Which domain filter should I pick?
faq.filter.a: New devices block malware by default, and ordinary sites are usually unaffected. The lists include HaGeZi's and Taiwanese government scam lists, and Quad9 judges the other lookups. The ad option occasionally breaks part of an ordinary site. To change it later, delete the device, create it again and import the new configuration file into the app.
faq.splitTunnel.q: Can I send only some apps through the VPN?
faq.splitTunnel.a: Yes, this is called split tunneling. When you edit a tunnel in AmneziaWG for Android, you can exclude apps or send only chosen apps through the VPN, for example to let a banking or work app connect directly. The iPhone and desktop apps have no per-app option. Apps left out of the VPN connect directly, so your network provider and whoever runs a public Wi-Fi can see where they go, and the domain filter does not apply to them. If unsure, keep the default and send all traffic through the VPN.
faq.noTraffic.q: The VPN says connected, but nothing loads?
faq.noTraffic.a: Like WireGuard, AmneziaWG shows "connected" as soon as you turn it on, without checking that the node answers. The connection details in the app show a "Latest handshake" time; if none appears, the node is not answering. Sign in to the portal and look at your devices: if this one is missing, it has expired and been deleted, so add a new one. A device marked "Paused" has used up this month's 50 GB and resumes on the 1st. If neither applies, the network you are on may be blocking the connection; try mobile data.
faq.trouble.a: Make sure AmneziaWG is up to date, then try another network, such as mobile data instead of Wi-Fi. If it still fails, delete the device and create it again. The disguise makes blocking less likely, but no network is guaranteed to work.
faq.speed.a: It depends on your network and how far you are from the node. In tests from Taiwan, the Taipei node had about 2 ms of latency, the Singapore node about 67 ms and about 200 Mbps; the Tokyo node about 180 Mbps down and 100 Mbps up.
faq.cities.q: Will there be nodes in other cities?
faq.cities.a: Singapore, Tokyo and Taipei for now. More will follow depending on how the service is used. You pick the city when you create a device; to switch cities, add another device.
faq.taipeiGeo.q: Why do some sites place the Taipei node in the Netherlands?
faq.taipeiGeo.a: Greenhost, which hosts the Taipei node, is a Dutch company, and some services wrongly place the node's IP address in the Netherlands for now, such as YouTube, Netflix and Google. Their region, language or catalogue may differ from Taiwan's, Facebook and Instagram may be slower, and services limited to Taiwanese IP addresses may not work. We are asking the host to get this corrected, which takes some time. Your connection and domain filtering are not affected.
faq.expire.a: Even if you stay connected, an account's devices expire after 30 days without opening the Vessel portal. Expired devices are deleted from the nodes and the device list, so unused configs do not linger on the nodes. Signing in, or opening the Vessel portal while signed in, extends them by 30 days, and opening it while connected to Vessel counts too. The device list shows each expiry date.
faq.expired.q: What happens after a device expires?
faq.expired.a: The account does not expire, and its number still signs you in. The expired device is gone from the node, so the config on your phone or computer no longer works; AmneziaWG may still say connected, but nothing gets through. Sign in, add a new device, import the new config, then delete the old entry in the app. Expired devices do not count toward the limit, and the service keeps no record of them, so they do not appear in the list.
faq.quota.a: The account's devices pause and resume automatically at 00:00 UTC on the 1st of the month. Nothing needs to be set up again.
faq.p2p.a: The terms ban BitTorrent and other P2P file sharing during the test. Nodes also block outgoing TCP port 25, so you cannot send mail straight to a mail server on port 25. Port 587, which mail apps normally use, is not affected.
faq.see.q: Can the service see what I do?
faq.see.a: Nodes handle the domains and IP addresses you connect to, but not the contents of HTTPS connections. Nodes keep no logs of them, and the DNS resolvers do not log queries. With a DNS filter, lookups go to Quad9 for a verdict. It sees the domain and the node's IP address, not yours. Using a VPN moves the trust you place in your network provider to the service. Use Tor Browser when you need anonymity. Only if you turn on a device inspection on a device are that device's connections copied to the community's analysis host, for at most 7 days.
faq.risky.q: Is Vessel safe to use where VPNs are restricted?
faq.risky.a: Some places restrict or ban unapproved VPNs, and using Vessel there can carry a penalty. In mainland China, police have publicly issued warnings and fines to individuals for using a VPN, and reports describe police going back through internet records from years earlier. Your local network provider can still see your device connecting to an IP address abroad and how much traffic passes, though not its content. The AmneziaWG app and its profile are also visible if someone inspects your device. If your situation is sensitive, check the local rules and risks before deciding to use it. When you need anonymity, you can use Tor Browser with a bridge instead, though Tor is restricted in some places too.
faq.risky.link: VPN and Tor conditions by location
faq.anomaly.q: What if I suspect unusual traffic from a device?
faq.anomaly.a: The device list shows each device's traffic this month, and for devices with a DNS filter, how many lookups the lists blocked. A device you rarely use with a lot of traffic, or a sudden jump in blocked lookups, suggests an app connecting in the background. The service only keeps the counts, so finding the cause takes a check on the device itself. If you suspect spyware, contact a digital security helpline.
faq.adId.q: How do I delete my phone's advertising ID?
faq.adId.a: Phones have a built-in advertising ID that apps and ad companies use to recognize the same phone across apps. It has also been used to target spyware attacks. Vessel's filter cannot do anything about it, so set it on the phone. On Android, go to Settings → Privacy → Ads and tap Delete advertising ID (search Settings for "ads" if you cannot find it). On iPhone, go to Settings → Privacy & Security → Tracking and turn off Allow Apps to Request to Track.
faq.law.q: What would the service hand over to law enforcement?
faq.law.a: Only what the privacy policy lists under the data we keep. The service keeps no connection logs, so it cannot tell which account used an exit IP at a given time. A device with an inspection turned on is the exception: during the inspection the analysis host holds that device's totals.
faq.cloudflare.q: Why does the portal go through Cloudflare?
faq.cloudflare.a: To stop attack traffic. Cloudflare can see visitors' IP addresses and the pages they view. VPN connections do not go through Cloudflare.
faq.tor.q: Can I open the portal in Tor Browser?
faq.tor.a: Yes. The portal has an onion site, its address at the foot of every page; it does not go through Cloudflare and sends no statistics. The portal needs JavaScript, which Tor Browser turns off at the Safest security level: the pages show, but you cannot sign in or send anything. Use Standard or Safer instead. The onion site cannot use passkeys; sign in with your account number.
faq.delete.q: How do I delete my account?
faq.delete.a: Delete it on the account page. All devices disconnect right away and the data is deleted with them. Database backups disappear after their retention period, which the privacy policy states.

dns.lead: When you create a device, you can have Vessel block malware sites and ads; blocking malware is the default. The filter works by domain (a site's name, such as example.com).

dns.check.ads: Using Vessel's DNS, blocking malicious sites, ads and trackers.

dns.lookup.body: When a site will not open, check here whether it is on Vessel's lists.
dns.lookup.label: Address or domain
dns.lookup.none: {domain} is not on Vessel's lists, so the lists are probably not the cause. The problem may be the site itself or your current network. If it opens with the VPN off, tell us through feedback.
dns.lookup.malware: {domain} is on the malware list. Devices with “Block malware” or “Block malware, ads and trackers” block it.
dns.lookup.ads: {domain} is on the ads and trackers list. Only devices with “Block malware, ads and trackers” block it.
dns.lookup.tw165: {domain} is on the 165 list of scam sites that Taiwan's National Police Agency has ISPs stop resolving, so Taiwan's ISPs do not resolve it either. Devices with “Block malware” or “Block malware, ads and trackers” block it.
dns.lookup.twmoda: {domain} is on the list of fake shops that Taiwan's Ministry of Digital Affairs has ISPs stop resolving, so Taiwan's ISPs do not resolve it either. Devices with “Block malware” or “Block malware, ads and trackers” block it.
dns.lookup.stalkerware: {domain} is on the list of stalkerware domains. Devices with “Block malware” or “Block malware, ads and trackers” block it.
dns.lookup.cti: {domain} is on DNSBunker's list of malicious domains. Devices with “Block malware” or “Block malware, ads and trackers” block it.
dns.lookup.reportNote: We check it and report it to the list's maintainer. If it is a mistake, we can add it to the exclusion list first.
dns.lookup.report165: Think this is a mistake? Taiwan's National Police Agency keeps this list; call the 165 anti-fraud hotline to appeal.
dns.lookup.reportModa: Think this is a mistake? The Administration for Digital Industries of Taiwan's Ministry of Digital Affairs keeps this list; appeal to them.
dns.lookup.privacy: Vessel does not store the addresses you look up or link them to your account. Lookups are checked with Quad9 and, from the regular address, pass through Cloudflare.
dns.options.title: The three options
dns.option.none: Only resolves domains and blocks nothing. Lookups do not go to Quad9.
dns.option.malware: Blocks domains that spread malware, phishing, scams and cryptomining, using HaGeZi Threat Intelligence Feeds (mini) and two Taiwanese government scam lists. Quad9 judges the other lookups.
dns.option.ads: Adds HaGeZi Multi PRO to block ad, tracking and analytics domains as well. It occasionally breaks part of an ordinary site.
dns.how.title: How it works
dns.how.body: Before your device connects to a site, it asks the DNS (the service that turns a site's name into an address) on Vessel's node. A domain on a list gets the answer "no such domain", so the connection is never made. Other lookups go to Quad9 over an encrypted connection, and domains Quad9 judges harmful get the same answer. The malware lists update every 6 to 8 hours and the ad and tracker list every day, and they are public on
dns.how.private: Vessel's DNS does not log lookups or which domains it blocked. Quad9 sees the domain and the node's IP address, not yours. The blocked count in your device list is only a number, and leaves out what Quad9 blocks.
dns.limits.title: What it cannot do
dns.limits.1: Ads served from the same domain as the content, such as ads in YouTube videos
dns.limits.2: The main domains of common services such as Facebook and YouTube are not on the lists, so ads and scam posts on them still appear
dns.limits.3: If your browser's Secure DNS is set by hand to another service, or an app sets its own DNS, the filter does not apply
dns.limits.4: It sees only domains, not the path of a URL or the contents of HTTPS connections
dns.limits.5: It does not replace antivirus software, and it can block an ordinary site
dns.change.title: Changing it and reporting mistakes
dns.change.body: You choose the filter when you create a device. To change it, delete the device, create it again and import the new configuration file into the app. If a site is wrongly blocked, confirm it with the lookup above and report it. We check it and report it to the list's maintainer, and if it is a mistake we can add it to the exclusion list first.

learn.title: VPN basics
learn.lead: What people using a VPN for the first time often ask.
learn.link: New to VPNs? Read the VPN basics
learn.what.title: What a VPN does
learn.what.1: When you go online, the networks your connection passes through can see which sites you visit: the Wi-Fi at a hotel or school, and your network provider.
learn.what.2: With the VPN on, your phone or computer encrypts the connection and sends it to Vessel's server first, which then connects to the site. The networks along the way only see that you connected to Vessel, not where you went next. Sites see the location of Vessel's server, and if you sign in to an account, they still know it is you.
learn.daily.title: Everyday use
learn.apps.title: Messaging, banking and Gmail
learn.apps.body: Most apps and sites work as usual. A few services, seeing a connection from another country, ask for an extra check, such as a text message code or a confirmation that it is really you. Just follow the prompts.
learn.stream.title: Streaming
learn.stream.body: Streaming services such as Netflix, Disney+ and HBO usually block VPN servers, so videos may not play while Vessel is on, and Vessel cannot be used to watch another country's catalogue. Turn the VPN off while you stream, and back on afterwards. On Android you can leave streaming apps out of the VPN.
learn.on.title: When to keep it on, and speed
learn.on.body: Keep it on when you use Wi-Fi at a café, hotel or school, and when you travel. It is usually a little slower than without it, and the battery difference is small. At home or on a network you trust, turn it off whenever you like.
learn.system.title: VPN options in your phone's settings
learn.system.android: On Android, go to Settings → Network & internet → VPN (the exact place varies by brand) and tap the gear next to AmneziaWG. There are two options. "Always-on VPN" connects to Vessel when the phone starts or the network comes back, and "Block connections without VPN" stops traffic while the VPN is down instead of letting it go out over the regular network. With both on, your traffic always goes through Vessel, but you cannot get online at all while the VPN is not connected. Only one app can be always-on at a time, so turn it off before you switch to another VPN.
learn.system.iphone: iPhone does not have these options. Some traffic from Apple's own services, such as Maps and the App Store, may go out directly instead of through the VPN. This is a limit of iOS itself and applies to every VPN app.
learn.working.title: Checking that it works
learn.working.body: Once the switch in AmneziaWG is on, open the connection check and press the button to confirm that your traffic goes through Vessel's server.
learn.trip.title: Getting ready for a trip
learn.trip.1: Before you leave, install AmneziaWG, create the device and test the connection at home. In some places the app stores do not have it, and the network may block it
learn.trip.2: If you will use both a phone and a laptop, create a device for each
learn.trip.3: Keep your account number in a password manager, or write it on paper and put it somewhere safe
learn.trip.4: While abroad, open vessel.anoni.net in a browser once while connected to Vessel to extend your devices by 30 days
learn.trip.5: Rules on using VPNs differ by country, so check the rules at your destination before you go
learn.trouble.title: When it will not connect
learn.trouble.1: If it stalls right after you leave Wi-Fi range or lose signal for a while, turn airplane mode on for a few seconds and then off again. Leave AmneziaWG on, so your traffic still goes through Vessel once the network is back
learn.trouble.2: If Android cannot get online at all, check whether "Block connections without VPN" is on in the VPN settings. It blocks all traffic while the VPN is not connected, so turning it off for now brings the connection back
learn.trouble.3: Try another network, for example mobile data instead of Wi-Fi
learn.trouble.4: Make sure AmneziaWG is updated to the latest version
learn.trouble.5: Check the status page to see whether the node is working
learn.trouble.6: If it still fails, tell us on the feedback page. Someone reads every message
learn.noticed.title: Whether others can tell it is a VPN
learn.noticed.body: Vessel disguises its connections, so ordinary network equipment has a hard time recognising them as a VPN, but equipment that analyses traffic closely may still tell. What it can learn is that you connected to Vessel's server, not where you went or what you sent. If you are at risk and need anonymity, use Tor Browser.
learn.see.title: What Vessel handles
learn.see.body: While you are connected, Vessel's server handles the sites you connect to, but cannot see what HTTPS encrypts, such as messages and passwords, and keeps no record of your connections. Only if you turn on a device inspection on a device are that device's connections copied to the community's analysis host, for at most 7 days.

lists.title: The lists behind the DNS filter
lists.lead: With DNS filtering on, Vessel blocks risky sites using the lists and Quad9's verdicts. If you are not sure which to pick, choose the recommended Block malware, which is also the default.
lists.choose.title: Which to pick
lists.choose.none: Blocks nothing, lookups do not go to Quad9, and the connection is still encrypted. Use it when you need to reach every site, or when another option blocks a site you need.
lists.choose.malware: Blocks sites that spread malware, phishing and scams. This suits most people, and ordinary sites are usually unaffected.
lists.choose.ads: Adds a larger list that blocks ads and trackers, and some more malware sites too. It occasionally breaks part of a site.
lists.trouble.title: When a site will not open
lists.trouble.2: If Vessel did not block it, the cause is probably the site or your current network. If it opens with the VPN off, the site may refuse VPN connections, or may have the node's location wrong. Tell us the address through
lists.trouble.3: If you need it urgently you can turn the VPN off, but a site on a list may really be harmful, so check the address before you pay. For a lasting fix, go to
lists.trouble.4: If you think it is a mistake, report it. For the 165 list (Taiwan police's anti-fraud hotline), call 165. For the Administration for Digital Industries list (part of Taiwan's Ministry of Digital Affairs), appeal to that agency. For other lists and Quad9, use
lists.trouble.note: Only the government can change its lists. If we confirm a mistake, Vessel can stop blocking the name on its own service and add it to the exclusion list. Vessel is run by volunteers and has no fixed response time.
lists.faq.title: Common questions
lists.faq.log.q: Does Vessel record which sites I look up?
lists.faq.log.a: No. Vessel's DNS keeps no record of lookups or of what it blocked. Filtering options send lookups to Quad9, which sees the domain and the node's IP address, not yours. The blocked count in your device list is only a number, and leaves out what Quad9 blocks. The node's configuration is public on GitHub. A device where you turned on an inspection is the exception: its lookups are copied to the community's analysis host during the inspection.
lists.faq.speed.q: Is it slower, or does it use more battery?
lists.faq.speed.a: The lists are compared on Vessel's servers, so your phone or computer does no extra matching and battery use should not change noticeably. On 2026-11-07 we measured all three nodes: lookups sent to Quad9 were no slower than without a filter, and most took under 0.1 seconds. We have not formally measured the difference in overall browsing speed. While a list updates, lookups can pause for a few seconds to a few tens of seconds.
lists.faq.sites.q: Will it block my bank, shopping sites or LINE?
lists.faq.sites.a: Usually not, though we have not checked banks and shopping sites one by one. In November 2026 we checked popular sites in Taiwan, Japan, Hong Kong and Singapore, and no main site was blocked. The lists can still be wrong, and Block malware, ads and trackers can break part of a site.
lists.faq.ads.q: Does it block ads inside apps?
lists.faq.ads.a: Some of them. Ads from the same domain as the content are not blocked, such as ads inside YouTube videos. When an app or browser looks up sites its own way, the filter does not apply.

lists.gov.2: The 165 list is requested by the police under the Fraud Crime Hazard Prevention Act, and the scam domain list comes from online retailers' reports. Taiwan's ISPs make these sites unreachable. On Vessel you would lose that protection, so we use the same lists.

lists.rules.title: The rules for choosing lists
lists.rules.1: Block security threats only. Ads and tracking are blocked only for people who choose that
lists.rules.2: No content control. Gambling, adult and social sites, circumvention tools and dynamic DNS (services that give a home network a fixed address) are not reasons to add a domain. Where a list includes them anyway, they are under known problems
lists.rules.3: We do not make our own block lists. We use only public lists and filtering services whose verdicts can be looked up, and report gaps to their maintainers
lists.rules.4: A new list has to add what the current ones lack, be checked for wrong blocks first, and come with terms that allow this use

lists.measure.title: The measurements in detail
lists.measure.lead: The share of phishing sites blocked a day after they first appeared, by who reported them.
lists.measure.how: Phishing: from 2026-11-01 to 11-08 we recorded sites newly reported by Poland's CERT Polska, OpenPhish and phishunt.io every hour and checked them then and 24 hours later, counting only sites that still resolved to an IP address. The nodes did not forward to Quad9 yet, so Vessel's share combines the results of the lists and Quad9. DNSBunker CTI is the hosting-platform subdomains on the list as of 2026-11-08, compared with the sites from this period. It shows what the list eventually held, not whether a site was blocked as soon as it appeared, so it counts only toward the share a day later.
lists.measure.bias: The reporting sources also feed some of the lists and Quad9, and a service that uses a source scores higher on it. phishunt.io is less affected, but has only about a hundred sites.
lists.measure.other: Malware: on 2026-11-07 we sampled 800 of malware-filter's URLhaus domains, counting only the 240 that still resolved to an IP address. Built-in tracking: measured on 2026-11-01, from HaGeZi's lists.
lists.measure.taiwan: Taiwan's scam sites: on 2026-11-07 we sampled 300 from each of the 165 list and the Administration for Digital Industries list, counting only sites that still resolved to an IP address (197 and 87, the second being a small sample).
lists.measure.date: We used only public lists and public test data, not anyone's lookups. Every service's results change, and the numbers only describe the time of measurement.

faq.phishing.a: It blocks only some phishing sites, so do not rely on it alone. Lists add sites afterwards, and for some reporting sources Vessel currently blocks fewer than Cloudflare's filtering service. Keep your browser's built-in phishing protection on, fill in passwords with a password manager, and use passkeys for important accounts.

lists.protect.title: Protection beyond the lists
lists.protect.lead: Lists add sites afterwards and DNS filtering only sees domains, so a new phishing site usually gets through. These three things do not wait for a list update.
lists.protect.1: Keep your browser's built-in phishing protection on: Chrome, Edge, Firefox and Safari all have it, usually on by default. It judges by address, not just the domain, so it has a chance of catching fake sites on shared platforms, and it exchanges data with the browser maker's service to do so.
lists.protect.2: Fill in passwords with a password manager: it only autofills on sites it has saved. If it does not autofill, check the address before you type anything.
lists.protect.3: Use passkeys for important accounts: a passkey is bound to the site's domain, so it does not work on a fake site.

inspect.title: Device traffic inspection
inspect.intro: If you want to know whether your phone or computer is connecting anywhere suspicious, you can turn on an inspection. For the next {days} days, a copy of this device's connections through Vessel goes to a community server for analysis. You can check the results so far at any time during the inspection, and download the full report when it ends.
inspect.collect.title: What is collected during the inspection
inspect.collect.names: The names of the sites and services your phone, computer and apps connect to, such as example.com
inspect.collect.where: Which server each connection went to, and when
inspect.collect.size: How much was uploaded and downloaded each hour
inspect.collect.packets: The start of each connection is copied in full, and after that only a small part of what is sent. Most sites and apps are encrypted: we can tell where they connect but cannot see messages, passwords, photos or other content.
inspect.collect.plain: On sites without encryption (browsers mark them “Not secure”) and in a few apps, what you send could be read by us, so please do not enter passwords or private information there during the inspection.
inspect.collect.not: We cannot tell which app made a connection. Your other devices are not inspected.
inspect.handling.title: How the data is handled
inspect.handling.whereValue: The community's analysis host in Tokyo, Japan
inspect.handling.packetsValue: Kept for about 20 minutes at most and deleted as soon as it is analysed. What remains is traffic totals, the names of sites on the malicious-site lists, and names that could not be found. No record is kept of the other sites you visited
inspect.handling.reportValue: Locked so that only this browser or the report key you saved can open it; we cannot read it either. Kept for {days} days after the end, so please download it. After that it is deleted, and the copy in backups, which cannot be opened, is gone within 14 days
inspect.handling.stopValue: You can end it at any time. Copying stops right away, and what remains is deleted once it is turned into your report
inspect.handling.group: Your group's leaders cannot see this report and are not told that you turned on an inspection.
inspect.handling.more: Full details in the privacy policy
